This is exactly the kind of rigorous, structural analysis we need right now. Read the full article in the SMU Law Review: scholar.smu.edu/cgi/viewcont…
For more on how immigration courts actually work, subscribe to my Substack: austinkocher.substack.com

The theoretical foundation here is Malcolm Feeley's classic "The Process is the Punishment." Chan inverts it for immigration: in removal proceedings, the process can also be the protection. Until it's engineered away.

Now the Trump administration is moving to strip away even this workaround, curtailing continuances, limiting administrative closures, and restricting judges' authority over detention. We're heading toward a system with no substantive relief AND no procedural escape valve.

Detention flips this logic completely. When someone is detained, time in the system stops being a benefit and becomes a punishment. Detention converts procedural delay from a de facto reprieve into an acute, ongoing harm.

The Biden "Dedicated Docket" is the clearest proof. Designed to speed up asylum cases, it accidentally exposed how much people had been benefiting from slow courts. Speed eliminated the informal protection that delays had been providing.

This is the core argument: procedural discretion quietly replaced substantive discretion. When you can't say "you can stay," you can say "come back in 18 months." The backlog wasn't just dysfunction, it was an improvised form of de facto relief.

So what did judges do? They improvised. Continuances, administrative closures, and docket delays became the primary way judges could give people something the law wouldn't let them formally give: more time in the United States while their cases dragged on.

Congress gutted the tools immigration judges had to grant relief from deportation, especially with the 1996 reforms. Judges lost the ability to weigh individual circumstances and grant status to people who clearly deserved it. The law moved away from individualized justice.

A new law review article just dropped that gets at something that has long been in conversation: immigration courts haven't just been backed up, the backlog has quietly been doing the work that the law no longer allows judges to do. Let me explain.

The memo reminds us that policy is made in two places: in the legal text and in the instructions officers actually receive. Those don't always match the press release. Reading the memo itself, not just the headlines, is the only way to know what's actually changing.

The memo explicitly signals USCIS will issue further category-specific guidance on particular AOS populations. This memo is the framework, not the full picture. What that means for parolees, specific visa categories, and others isn't settled yet. Watch this space.

Attorneys at Boundless reviewed the full memo and say they'll keep filing AOS cases. Their near-term concern: more RFEs and written denials as officers document discretionary reasoning. Processing will likely slow. That's different from a categorical bar but it's real.

H-1B, L-1, and other dual-intent visa holders can still apply. But the memo is direct: maintaining lawful dual-intent status is "not sufficient, on its own, to warrant a favorable exercise of discretion." A clean record helps. It doesn't guarantee approval.

The memo states: if you entered on a temporary visa or parole and stayed to adjust instead of departing, that itself is an adverse factor. Per PM-602-0199 p.5, citing Matter of Blas, applicants may need to show "unusual or even outstanding equities" to overcome it.

The memo tells officers: meeting eligibility requirements gets you in the door. It doesn't mean you get approved. Officers must now actively weigh negative factors,status violations, overstays, conduct inconsistent with the purpose of admission, not just check eligibility boxes.

PM-602-0199 is internal guidance, instructions to USCIS officers about how to think about cases. It doesn't change statute, eliminate any green card category, or create new eligibility rules. What it changes is the posture officers are told to bring to every adjudication.

USCIS issued PM-602-0199 on May 21. The press release said AOS would be granted "only in extraordinary circumstances." That phrase appears nowhere in the actual memo. The gap between the political statement and the operative policy is worth understanding. A thread.

The DHS data is public. The vote record is public. The cases are on the record. We are watching a system that sees the problem, acknowledges it, and declines to act. I don't know what to call that but I know what it isn't. 

Link:austinkocher.substack.com

As a Navy veteran who served during Afghanistan and Iraq, I find it hard to describe how strange it is to be writing this on the eve of Memorial Day. Both parties nominally agree this is wrong. What's missing is the will to make that mean something in law.
